newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO says it alert to Serb threats in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: NATO says it alert to Serb threats in Bosnia.

text.p: A U.S. soldier suffered minor injuries in a stabbing attack in Bosnian Serb-controlled territory on Wednesday as NATO warned it was alert to possible retaliation for a raid on indicted war criminals.
The American soldier was stabbed in the left shoulder before dawn on Wednesday outside his living quarters by a man wielding a hand-sickle, the NATO-led peace force said.

The soldier suffered a two to three inch (six centimetre) cut in his left shoulder in the attack, which occurred in the Kladanj region, about 80 km (50 miles) north of Sarajevo. He returned to his unit later in the day after being treated by military doctors.
The stabbing followed three bombings in three days targeting unarmed international monitors in apparent retaliation for a tougher NATO policy on indicted war criminals.

The latest explosion occurred early on Wednesday outside the offices and apartment of a United Nations police monitor in Prijedor, where British soldiers pounced on two suspected war criminals last week.
The blasts have caused no injuries but underlined concerns about a potential Serb backlash to the NATO action against two Serbs wanted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.

British special forces arrested one suspect last Thursday and shot dead another who resisted and opened fire. Both men were charged in sealed indictments for leading "ethnic cleansing" against Moslems and Croats early in the Bosnian war in the Prijedor region.
NATO officers said there was no evidence of an orchestrated revenge campaign and said the stabbing was still under investigation.
The 31,000-strong Stabilisation Force (SFOR) also said it received a letter calling on Serbs to retaliate for the raid.
"We received a piece of paper and it's entitled a 'proclamation' addressed to the Serb nation which appears to be a threat against SFOR troops," spokesman Major John Blakeley said..

He declined to divulge details of the letter but said: "Suffice it to say while there are certain threats to SFOR our forces are well-trained, well-equipped and have robust rules of engagement to deal with any situation which may arise."
SFOR said necessary security precautions had been taken where necessary but said the situation remained "calm".

Serb leaders have condemned the NATO action as unjust but have refrained from inciting violence in public statements. During the 1992-95 Bosnian war, Serb forces fired on U.N. soldiers and took them hostage to prevent NATO air strikes.
NATO now strictly supervises Bosnia's rival armies, obliging them to keep heavy weapons in storage sites and obtain permission to move troops.
The Serb leadership has also protested at the use of sealed, or secret, indictments in the swoop and alleged that NATO possessed a "secret list" of suspects.
NATO said that the contents of other sealed indictments were known only to tribunal prosecutors. "There is no secret list," Blakeley said.
The introduction of sealed indictments has set off a wave of speculation in the press throughout former Yugoslavia about who may be arrested next.
Nationalist Serb leaders fear the arrest operation by the British may have been a test run for a swoop on former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic and his army commander, General Ratko Mladic.
France denied a report in the New York Times that it had rejected a plan to snatch Karadzic, one of 67 suspects on a published list of indictees who remain at large.
Since the peace agreement was signed in 1995, Karadzic has stayed in his headquarters in the mountain village of Pale, outside Sarajevo, continuing to wield power behind the scenes.
Mladic has kept out of the public spotlight, spending his time both in Bosnia's Serb Republic and in the Yugoslav capital Belgrade, where his family lives in an affluent suburb.
